newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - French dialogue seeks to humanise European Union.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - French dialogue seeks to humanise European Union.

text.p: The rolling pastures of the bucolic Creuse region are, in more senses than one, the dead centre of France.

This agrarian Bermuda triangle, euphemistically designated a Rural Revitalisation Zone, has suffered so badly from poverty and depopulation that local mayors last year founded a mock Creuse National Liberation Front (FLNC).

They borrowed the acronym, if not the violent tactics, of Corsican separatist guerrillas to dramatise their plight by comparing it to the French Mediterranean island, where the government had just won European Commission permission to establish a tax-haven enterprise zone.

So it took courage for Michel Barnier, France's European affairs minister, to bring his "National Dialogue for Europe" to the Creuse, which voted by a hefty 56 percent against the Maastricht treaty on European Union in a 1992 referendum. French voters as a whole approved the treaty by 51.05 percent.

"We feel far removed from the arc of prosperity that stretches from southern England to northern Italy," lamented Aubusson mayor Pierre-Henri Bos on welcoming Barnier to this town reputed for centuries for its tapestries.

"The people of the Creuse have contradictory feelings about Europe," said Gaullist parliamentarian Bernard de Froment, who heads the Creuse district council. "They are aware of receiving EU aid, but they are suspicious of remote Brussels technocracy. It is easy for farmers to blame their problems on Brussels."
LOCALS FEAR DECLINE
Froment acknowledged that French politicians mask the scale of EU aid by taking credit themselves for EU-funded projects.

Yet both he and Bos complained that the Creuse, with a per capita gross domestic product just 68 percent of the EU average, does not get as much European aid as it should because it is lumped in a single region with the richer cities of Limoges and Brive.
"We need better differentiated aid," Bos said.
The questions Barnier faced from an audience of high-school students and teachers in Aubusson highlighted local fears.

"The weak are being wiped out. Small businesses, small farmers and even the local building training college are closing down. Will we young people be able to live and work in this area?" asked Sabrina, a final-year student.

"It's not fair to say all this is the European Union's fault," Barnier replied. "Cutting back the building college was a national decision...It's true we have lost many farms, but that process began a century ago, and without the EU Common Agricultural Policy it would have been far worse."
He noted that the Creuse was set to receive 200 million francs ($37 million) over the 1994-98 period in EU structural funds, in addition to regular aid to farmers.
"The Creuse is one of the regions that will continue to need European aid for a long time, even if some other regions will have to prepare to receive less," the minister said.
Some of the Creuse's problems, such as a slump in beef consumption because of public fears over mad cow disease, were due to the fact that the EU had too little power, not too much.
MINISTER INVITES EU DEBATE AROUND FRANCE

Every Thursday, Barnier, best known to French voters as the organiser of the 1992 Albertville Winter Olympics, visits a different region of France to encourage debate and even invite controversy about the EU.
His aim, he says, is to keep President Jacques Chirac's campaign pledge to "reconcile the French people with Europe and about Europe".
"Europe has been built for 40 years by statesmen and diplomats but ordinary people have rarely had their say. We need to involve people more," Barnier told reporters.
"Nothing is worse than silence. I want people to talk about Europe regularly, not just when there is a crisis like mad cow disease, or a war such as Bosnia."

To illustrate wider enthusiasm for the EU, Barnier took along on his trip the Paris ambassadors of Austria, which recently joined the Union, and of two countries clamouring to get in -- Slovakia and Cyprus.

On his next stop in Gueret, the administrative centre of the Creuse, Barnier inaugurated a committee to promote the euro, the single European currency due to come into force in 1999 and enter citizens' pockets in 2002.

Then he joined Edith Cresson, European commissioner for education and training and a former French prime minister, for a public debate with 600 trade unionists, employers, elected officials and students at an EU-funded technology park in Limoges.

The trade unionists were angry that Brussels was undermining their ideal of public services by forcing France to accept private competition with the state monopoly in electricity, gas, telecommunications and, they fear, railways.
They also expressed concern that the EU was undermining France's social model by forcing it to compete with countries such as Britain that have less generous social protection.
OPPONENTS WANT SOCIAL COHESION BESIDES EURO

Robert Savy, Socialist president of the Limousin regional council, which includes the Creuse, said the European Union would have to develop stronger social cohesion and do more for underdeveloped areas if people were not to reject it.
"Europe will fail if it is simply a means of adapting the continent to ultra-liberal globalisation, because citizens will make it a scapegoat for their difficulties," Savy said.

"For it to succeed, we need a European project in which all groups of the population and all regions find their place. That is the price of social peace, indeed of peace itself," he said. "Europe must be more than just the euro."
Barnier argued that the EU provided the best chance of achieving common standards for workers' rights and welfare protection to prevent unfair competition.
"There is no hostility to the European ideal in France, but people are asking "will the EU help us find jobs' or "will the EU protect our social system'", he said.
"The anwer is that Europe is going to help protect us from the impact of globalisation."
